lesson.title: Guess-the-Gender Game
lesson.subtitle: Unseen words, suffix laws, explanation feedback — the exam of the suffix court

hook.title: Unseen Words, Known Laws
hook.content: Today's words were deliberately never taught. That is the point. You will meet Zeitung, Gesundheit, Lehrer, Zwilling, Mädchen — words from the wild — and guess their gender from the suffix alone. der? die? das? The laws you own: -ung/-heit/-keit/-schaft → die, -chen/-lein → das, verb+-er → der, plain -e → usually die, -zeug → das. Guess, then read the explanation: every answer teaches the law behind the word. This is the exam where guessing IS the method.

footnotes.title: Why Guessing Works
footnotes.content: German gender is roughly half suffix-predictable, and the suffixes cover exactly the high-frequency vocabulary. Guessing from suffixes beats memorizing articles one by one — and every wrong guess still installs the law.

pattern.title: The Exam Walkthrough
pattern.content: die Zeitung — Zeit + ung: the -ung factory. die Gesundheit — gesund + heit. der Lehrer — lehren (to teach) + er: the agent law. der Zwilling — the -ling law (your twin word!). das Mädchen — the -chen law, the famous paradox. die Butter — plain -e, usually feminine. das Feuerzeug — the -zeug law. der Montag? weekdays end in Tag — der by the head-word law. Each guess activates a law; each law covers thousands of words. Score yourself, then re-read the suffix court from the Gender Heuristics lesson.
pattern.linguist_note: The suffix laws are historical regularities, not dictionary conventions: -ung nouns are feminine because the suffix itself was feminine in Proto-Germanic. The laws predate the dictionary — which is why they still hold.

exercises.prompt: Unseen word: 'die Zeitung' (newspaper). Which law made it feminine?
exercises.meaning: die Zeitung — the -ung law at work
exercises.explanation: Zeitung is literally 'a timing' — your taught word Zeit with the feminine -ung stamp.

options: verb + -er: the agent law, always der
exercises.target_answer: verb + -er: the agent law, always der
exercises.explanation: lehren (to teach) + -er → der. Same factory as der Sauger (dust-sucker) and der Fernseher (far-seer).

exercises.prompt: Unseen word: 'das Mädchen' (girl). Which law outranks the meaning?
exercises.explanation: The diminutive -chen is the most exceptionless gender law in German — even 'the girl' becomes das.
Your own twin word! The -ling suffix (duckling's German sister) stamps masculine: der Zwilling, der Lehrling (apprentice).

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the German sentence you hear:
exercises.meaning: Die Zeitung ist gut = The newspaper is good
exercises.explanation: One unseen word, one law, one correct article — the guess-the-gender method paying out.
cues: Meaning: "Die Zeitung ist gut = The newspaper is good"
Opens with "Die Zeitung" and ends with "gut".

summary.outcome: Guess the gender of unseen nouns from suffix laws and explain every choice.
summary.takeaway: -ung/-heit/-keit/-schaft → die, -chen/-zeug → das, -er/-ling → der — the laws cover the wild.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: plurals & i-mutation — Mann becomes Männer the way man becomes men: umlaut is English's own fossil.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Guess-the-Gender Game (Die Zeitung ist gut = The newspaper is good):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Die Zeitung ist gut" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Guess-the-Gender Game without relying on short-term echo.

wahrnehmung.etymology_derivation: Calque of Latin perceptio (wahr = true + nehmen = take → taking as true).

zeit.etymology_derivation: t → z [ts] (cognate with English "tide", as in Yuletide or time and tide).

straße.etymology_derivation: Roman paved road (via strata) gave English "street" (kept Latin "t") and German "Straße" (shifted "t" to sharp "ß").

butter.etymology_derivation: Borrowed together into West Germanic from Latin butyrum / Greek boutyron.

zwilling.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *twinaz (two, twinned) + the Germanic suffix -ling (as in duckling); English twin is the same root without the suffix. [wiktionary]

frau.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *frawjǭ 'lady, mistress' — kin to archaic English frow 'lady'; Fräulein andMs.-style Frauennamen carry the same root. [wiktionary]

mann.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *mann- — the identical twin of man; German keeps the short a English lengthened. [wiktionary]

kind.context_translation: The child plays in the garden.
kind.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *kindą, related to the root of English kin — 'of the family'. The t → z shift never fired here; the d hardened to t instead. [wiktionary]

kühl.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *kōluz — cognate with English cool (the umlaut is German's own). [wiktionary]

knopf.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *knuppaz 'lump'; English button is unrelated — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

zitrone.context_phrase: Der Tee mit Zitrone schmeckt gut.
zitrone.context_translation: The tea with lemon tastes good.
zitrone.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Italian citrone and Middle French citron, from Latin citrus; English citron and citrus come from the same Latin word. [wiktionary]

höflich.etymology_derivation: Hof (court, farm) plus -lich, literally courtly, in the manner of the court; the entry parallels it with Old French cortois, which gave English courteous — polite speech learned at court in both languages. [wiktionary]

körper.context_phrase: Der menschliche Körper hat viele Knochen.
körper.context_translation: The human body has many bones.
körper.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German korper, from Latin corpor-, the stem of corpus. English corpse is the direct cognate. [wiktionary]

rezept.context_phrase: Der Arzt schreibt mir ein Rezept.
rezept.context_translation: The doctor writes me a prescription.
rezept.etymology_derivation: From earlier recept, from Latin receptus; the page states it is cognate with English receipt — recipe is just the cooking variant of the same word. [wiktionary]

priester.context_phrase: Der Priester wohnt neben der Kirche.
priester.context_translation: The priest lives next to the church.
priester.etymology_derivation: Both English priest and German Priester go back to Latin presbyter, from Greek presbyteros, elder - the same ecclesiastical loan, borrowed into German around the year 700. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
